Tuesday evening. Ioana phones Monsieur Garnier, the man who sold them the piano. She wants to find out who Hélène from the envelope in the piano is.
Good evening, Monsieur Garnier. This is Ioana Popescu. My partner bought a piano from you last week.
Ah yes, the old Pleyel! Is there a problem?
No, it’s perfect. But we found an envelope inside. A score, with “For Hélène, Lyon, 1962”.
Hélène? That’s my aunt, Hélène Morel! The piano was hers. She’s eighty-three. She lives in a care home in Fourvière.
Do you think she’ll be glad to get the score back?
Oh yes! She’ll cry with joy, I’m sure of it. I’ll call her tomorrow morning and explain everything.
Will we be able to visit her?
Of course, she loves visitors. Will you go on Saturday? I’ll let the nurse know.
Saturday is perfect. We’ll come at about three o’clock.
I’ll send you the address by text. And your partner, will he be able to play the waltz?
He already plays it every evening! He’s a music teacher.
Then make a recording. She doesn’t have a piano any more. She’ll be so happy to hear it!
(Ioana hangs up.) Well? What did he say?
Hélène exists! On Saturday we’re going to see her. You’ll record the waltz, and I’ll buy flowers.
And what will we tell her?
The truth. That her piano will be happy with us. And that we’ll be happy with it.

The middle e almost disappears: “zhuh parl-RAY”. The ending -rai is read “ray”, with a closed é.
“Noo suh-RÕ”: -ons is nasal, as in “bon”. “Ils seront” sounds the same (“eel suh-RÕ”); only the pronoun tells them apart.
“Zhuh fuh-RAY”: the e in fe- is read like a short “uh”, not like é. Careful: not “je féré”.
“Zhã-ve-RAY”: the double r is read as one. Likewise “je verrai” (I’ll see) = “zhuh ve-RAY”, “je pourrai” = “zhuh poo-RAY”.
1. How the futur simple is formed
Good news: almost all verbs use the INFINITIVE as the stem, and you add the endings. And the endings look like the present of “avoir” (ai, as, a, avons → ons, avez → ez, ont).
Verbs in -re drop their final e: prendre → prendr- → je prendrai; écrire → j’écrirai; boire → je boirai. Every future form has an R before the ending!
English has “I will speak” / “I’m going to speak”. French also has two options: “je parlerai” (futur simple) and “je vais parler” (futur proche, chapter 9).
Some verbs have a special stem, but the endings stay the same. These are the most common ones and worth learning by heart:
Like venir: tenir → je tiendrai, revenir → je reviendrai, devenir → je deviendrai, prévenir → je préviendrai.
Some -er verbs change their spelling slightly, as in the present: acheter → j’achèterai, appeler → j’appellerai, jeter → je jetterai, payer → je paierai (or payerai).
Both express the future. The difference is one of nuance, like English “I’m going to leave” and “I will leave”:
Demain, il pleuvra dans le nord.
Promises are almost always made in the futur simple: “Je te le promets, je serai là.” (I promise, I’ll be there.) “Je ne le ferai plus !” (I won’t do it again!)
When you come to Iași, I’ll show you the city.
When I have time, I’ll read this book.
If the weather’s nice on Saturday, we’ll walk.
If you like, I’ll help you.

After QUAND (referring to the future) French requires the FUTURE, unlike English: “Quand tu viendras” (not “quand tu viens”). But after SI you NEVER use the future, just like English: “Si tu viens” (not “si tu viendras”)!
dans trois jours / dans deux ans
in three days / in two years’ time
un jour / un de ces jours
one day / one of these days
“Dans” + duration = in (the future): “dans deux ans” = in two years’ time. Don’t confuse it with “il y a deux ans” = two years ago (in the past).
They’ll take the eight o’clock train.
When you arrive in Lyon, I’ll show you Vieux Lyon.
Si tu viendras, je te montrerai.
Si tu viens, je te montrerai.
Quand tu viens, je te montre.

On Saturday at three o’clock, Ioana and Julien went up to Fourvière. Ioana was carrying a bouquet of white roses. Julien had the score in his bag and the recording on his phone.
The care home was an old building with a big garden. From up there you could see the whole city. The nurse took them to room number twelve.
Hélène Morel was sitting by the window. She was small, with completely white hair and very blue eyes. She was wearing an elegant dress, as if for a party.
“So you’re the young people who’ve adopted my piano?” she asked with a smile. “My nephew told me everything. Sit down, sit down!”
Julien took out the yellow envelope and handed it to her. Hélène opened it slowly. Her hands were trembling a little. When she saw the score, she said nothing for a long minute.
“I thought it was lost forever,” she said at last. “I looked for it everywhere when I left my flat.”
Then Julien played the recording. The waltz filled the little room. Hélène closed her eyes. She was gently moving her hand, as if she were dancing.
When the music stopped, she opened her eyes. They were full of tears, but she was smiling.
“A boy wrote this waltz for me. I was twenty. He was twenty-two. He was a music student, and he played divinely.”
“We wanted to get married. He always used to say: ‘One day we’ll have a house with a piano, and I’ll play you this waltz every evening.’”
“And then he left to do his military service, in Algeria. He promised me: ‘I’ll come back.’ But when the war ended, he didn’t come back to Lyon. His letters stopped. I never saw him again.”
There was a long silence. Ioana took Hélène’s hand. “What was his name?” she asked softly.
“Henri. Henri Bernard. He came from Marseille.” Hélène smiled sadly. “He must have had a good life, somewhere. I hope so.”
Ioana and Julien looked at each other. They were thinking of the same person: their neighbour, Madame Bernard, who came from Marseille… and whose husband, who died five years ago, was called Henri.
They said nothing. Not yet. As they left, Julien promised: “We’ll come back next week. And one day you’ll come to our place to listen to your piano.” Hélène replied: “I’ll come. I promise.”
